newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSIGHT-AUSSIE DOLLAR SETS ITS SIGHTS ON US$0.75.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT-AUSSIE DOLLAR SETS ITS SIGHTS ON US$0.75.

text.p: *Offshore selling clears weak long positions, but dollar recovers to where it closed local trading on Wednesday as U.S. buyers continued to appear.
*Next target past US$0.7460 is US$0.7500, and the fact that dollar has posted three successive higher closes this week seen as a positive sign.

The Australian dollar was looking to set itself up for an attempt on US$0.7500, a level it was last above in early July, after a solid performance that has seen it rise about one and a half cents this week.

When Wednesday's unexpected rally ran into resistance at US$0.7460, offshore profit-takers took the dollar back down below US$0.7420, as many traders had expected given the rally was driven by one major buyer.
However, fund buyers appeared at the low and took it back above US$0.7450. By 8.00 a.m. (2200 GMT) the dollar was at US$0.7456/61, almost level with Wednesday's late US$0.7453/58.
The dollar was finding good support in early local trading, and traders said the bias on the day was to the upside.
If the dollar managed to clear US$0.7460, the unit would target US$0.7500, analysts said, with solid resistance expected from US$0.7485.
The dollar last tried to make a break above US$0.7500 in late July, but was rebuffed and declined over the first week of August, culminating in last Friday's two year lows of US$0.7295.
Since then, however, the dollar has posted higher closes each day, and has found itself well-supported after moving through numerous resistance levels.
On the crosses, losses in the U.S. dollar on concerns of possible higher German interest rates and delays in European Monetary Union saw the Australian dollar lose some ground.
The Australian dollar opened at 86.19/29 yen and 1.3677/94 marks, down on late local levels on Wednesday of 86.69/79 and 1.3820/37.

Data out on Thursday will update the market on the pace of wages growth, although given the recent July 30 rate cut, it is not expected to have a significant market impact. Economists expect the data to show that wages are not an obstacle to further interest rate cuts if the RBA saw one as necessary.

Preliminary data released last month showed a 0.5 percent quarterly rise, leading the annual rate to moderate to 3.7 percent, well below the level considered to be the RBA's line in the sand on wages growth, 4.5 percent.

The final data also provides a split between the pace of private and public sectors wages growth. The controlled pace of private sector wages over the past year has been one of the factors that gave the RBA room to ease, and economists expect annual growth to remain below 4.0 percent.
